title: Daoism: The Way and Effortless Action
subtitle: Why the softest thing in the world overcomes the hardest
era: c. 4th–3rd century BCE (texts); legend places Laozi in the 6th century BCE
objectives: By the end you will be able to explain the key terms dao, de, wu wei, ziran and pu in the Dao De Jing
By the end you will be able to analyse how the Dao De Jing uses paradox, reversal and images such as water and emptiness
By the end you will be able to interpret Zhuangzi's butterfly dream and Cook Ding story and compare relativist, skeptical and perspectivist readings
By the end you will be able to evaluate the Daoist critique of Confucian ritual and of striving itself
hook:
A butcher named Ding is carving an ox for his lord. Every movement of his hand, shoulder and knee is in rhythm, like a dance. Asked how he got so skilful, he says that at first he saw nothing but the whole ox; after three years he no longer saw the ox as a whole; now he meets it with his spirit rather than his eyes, and his blade slides through the natural gaps between the joints. A good cook changes his knife once a year because he cuts; an ordinary cook once a month because he hacks. Ding has used the same blade for nineteen years, and its edge is still as if fresh from the whetstone.

This story comes from the *Zhuangzi*, one of the two great classics of early Daoism. On Day 87 you met Laozi briefly as a voice of quiet paradox. This lesson goes further. Daoism asks a disturbing question of everything we usually call effort, ambition and moral improvement. What if the problem is not that we try too little, but that we try at all, in the wrong way? What if the deepest skill, in carving, in governing, in living, comes from getting yourself out of the way?

sections.heading: Laozi, a Text and a Legend
sections.body:
Tradition says that **Laozi** ('Old Master') was an archivist at the Zhou court, an older contemporary of Kongzi, who, disgusted at the decline of the realm, rode west on an ox. At the border pass a guard begged him to write down his wisdom, and he left behind a short book of about five thousand characters before vanishing. Already the historian Sima Qian (c. 145–c. 86 BCE), who records this story, admitted uncertainty about who Laozi was. Most scholars today treat the story as legend and the text as a compilation, built up from earlier sayings and reaching something like its present form by around the third century BCE. Bamboo slips discovered at Guodian in 1993, buried around 300 BCE, contain about a third of the text, in a different order, which supports this picture of gradual growth.

The book is the **Dao De Jing** (*Tao Te Ching* in older spelling), 'the Classic of the Way and Its Power'. It has 81 short chapters, mostly in rhyming verse. It has been translated into Western languages more often than almost any book except the Bible, and the translations differ wildly, because the classical Chinese is terse, has no tenses or plurals, and is deliberately ambiguous.

A note on labels. Later Chinese scholars distinguished **daojia** (the 'school of the Way', meaning these philosophical texts) from **daojiao** (the organised religion with temples, priests and practices of longevity that emerged from the second century CE). Many scholars now think this sharp split is a Western convenience; the religion treats Laozi as divine and reveres the texts. But this lesson focuses on the philosophical ideas in the two classics.

sections.heading: The Dao That Cannot Be Named
sections.body:
**Dao** (道) literally means 'way' or 'path', and by extension a method, a teaching or a way of speaking. Kongzi's Dao was the way of the ancient sages, a social and ethical path. The *Dao De Jing* turns the word into something vaster: the source and pattern of all things, prior to Heaven and Earth.

Its first chapter opens with a famous warning, often rendered: the way that can be spoken of is not the constant way; the name that can be named is not the constant name. A pun is buried here, because *dao* also means 'to speak'. Any dao we can *dao* (any way we can put into words) is not the enduring one. Language carves the world into fixed categories, and the Dao is what is there before and beneath the carving.

This is not quite like Plato's Form of the Good (Day 11) or Parmenides's unchanging Being (Day 5). The Dao is not a perfect, static object beyond the changing world. It is more like the pattern of change itself, closer in spirit to Heraclitus's logos in flux (Day 4), but with a crucial difference in tone: the Dao is described with feminine and nurturing images. It is the 'mother' of the ten thousand things, the 'valley spirit' that never dies, the dark, receptive origin.

**De** (德) means virtue or power, the potency something has when it is in accord with the Dao. A person of great de does not show off their virtue; chapter 38 says the highest de does not regard itself as de, and that is why it has de. When the Dao is lost, the text goes on, people fall back on de; when de is lost, on humaneness (ren); then rightness (yi); then ritual (li), which it calls the thinning of loyalty and trust and the beginning of disorder. Here the *Dao De Jing* turns Confucian values upside down: the virtues that Kongzi preached are symptoms of a lost way, not cures.

sections.heading: Wu Wei, Water and the Uses of Emptiness
sections.body:
The central practical ideal is **wu wei** (無為), literally 'no action' or 'non-doing'. It does not mean laziness or passivity. It means action without forcing, striving or self-conscious control: action that flows from the situation, like Cook Ding's knife. Chapter 37 states the paradox: the Dao never acts, yet nothing is left undone.

The text's favourite image is **water**. The highest good is like water, says chapter 8: it benefits the ten thousand things without contending, and settles in low places that people despise. Chapter 78 adds that nothing in the world is softer or weaker than water, yet nothing is better at attacking the hard and strong. Think of a river canyon: carved not by force but by persistent yielding.

A second image is **emptiness**. Chapter 11 observes that thirty spokes share one hub, but it is the empty space at the centre that makes the wheel useful; we shape clay into a pot, but it is the hollow inside that makes it useful; we cut doors and windows, and it is the empty spaces that make a room. Being gives benefit, non-being gives use. Western philosophy has mostly prized presence and substance (Aristotle's *ousia* on Day 18); the *Dao De Jing* draws attention to the productive role of absence.

Related ideals include **ziran** (自然), 'self-so' or spontaneity, the way things are of themselves when not interfered with, and **pu** (樸), the 'uncarved block', a symbol of simplicity before social shaping. Recall Xunzi's image of crooked wood that must be steamed straight (World track, lesson 1). The *Dao De Jing* inverts it: the carving is the problem.

The text also notices **reversal**. Chapter 2 points out that when everyone recognises beauty as beauty, ugliness has thereby been established; high and low, long and short, before and after give rise to one another. Opposites depend on each other and pass into each other, so clinging to one pole is futile. Hence advice that sounds backwards: the sage puts himself last and finds himself first; bending, you become whole.

sections.heading: Government by Not Governing
sections.body:
Strikingly, much of the *Dao De Jing* is addressed to rulers. Its politics follows from wu wei. Chapter 17 ranks rulers: the best are those whose people barely know they exist; next, those they love and praise; next, those they fear; worst, those they despise. When the best ruler's work is done, the people all say it happened of itself (*ziran*).

Chapter 60 compares governing a large state to cooking a small fish: poke it too much and it falls apart. Chapter 57 warns that the more prohibitions there are, the poorer the people; the more laws are promulgated, the more thieves and bandits there are. Chapter 80 imagines a small state with few people, where boats and carriages go unused, people are content with their food and customs, and though the next village is within earshot they never visit.

Interpreters disagree about how to read this. Some see a kind of proto-anarchism or libertarian minimalism, and indeed later Chinese texts used Daoist ideas to argue against heavy taxation. Others notice darker lines: chapter 3 says the sage empties people's minds and fills their bellies, weakens their ambitions and strengthens their bones, keeping them without cunning knowledge. A cynical ruler could read this as a manual for keeping subjects docile. The early Han court in fact adopted a 'Huang-Lao' Daoist policy of light government in the second century BCE, before turning to Confucianism.

Compare Wolff's philosophical anarchism from the Political track: both distrust command. But Wolff's argument rests on individual autonomy and rational self-legislation, while the *Dao De Jing* rests on a cosmology in which things go best when left to their own nature. It would be a mistake to translate one into the other.

sections.heading: Zhuangzi: Butterflies, Fish and the Equality of Things
sections.body:
**Zhuangzi** (Zhuang Zhou, c. 369–c. 286 BCE) is a very different writer: funny, wild, full of talking trees, giant birds and philosophers who lose arguments to cripples and thieves. The book bearing his name has 33 chapters; most scholars think the first seven, the 'Inner Chapters', are closest to his own thought, with the rest added by followers.

The second chapter, 'Discussion on Making Things Equal' (*Qiwulun*), ends with the most famous dream in Chinese literature. Zhuang Zhou dreamt he was a butterfly, flitting about happily, not knowing he was Zhou. Suddenly he woke, and there he was, Zhou. But he did not know whether he was Zhou who had dreamt he was a butterfly, or a butterfly dreaming he was Zhou. Yet, the passage adds, between Zhou and a butterfly there must be some distinction. This, it says, is called **the transformation of things** (*wuhua*).

Compare Descartes's dream argument (Day 43). Descartes used dreaming to doubt, then sought a foundation that would end doubt. Zhuangzi does not seem anxious at all. The point may not be 'I cannot know which is real' but 'I can be at ease in either', since life is a stream of transformations: Zhou into butterfly, life into death. When his wife died, a friend found Zhuangzi drumming on a pot and singing; he explained that after his first grief he reflected that her life had been one transformation and her death another, like the turning of the seasons (chapter 18, an outer chapter).

The same chapter attacks the endless disputes between Confucians and Mohists. Each calls 'right' (*shi*) what the other calls 'wrong' (*fei*). But every judgement is made from a standpoint. Humans sleep in damp places and get backache; is that true of eels? Humans perch in trees and tremble; is that true of monkeys? Which of the three knows the right place to live? The sage, Zhuangzi suggests, stands at the **pivot of the Dao** (*daoshu*), the centre of the circle from which all perspectives can be seen and none is clung to.

With his logician friend **Huizi**, Zhuangzi argued over a bridge (chapter 17). Zhuangzi said: see how the minnows dart about; that is the happiness of fish. Huizi: you are not a fish, how do you know what fish enjoy? Zhuangzi: you are not me, how do you know I don't know? The exchange ends with a joke about the word 'how', and readers still argue whether it is sophistry or a profound point about knowledge from within a lived encounter.

sections.heading: Relativist, Skeptic, or Something Else?
sections.body:
So what is Zhuangzi's position? Scholars disagree, and the disagreement is instructive.

On a **relativist** reading (associated with Chad Hansen), Zhuangzi holds that there is no perspective-free standard of right and wrong: every *shi/fei* judgement is relative to a way of carving up the world. The obvious objection is the one Plato raised against Protagoras (Day 8): if all views are equally valid, so is the view that relativism is false. And Zhuangzi plainly prefers some ways of living (Cook Ding's) to others (the anxious striving of officials).

On a **skeptical** reading (developed by Paul Kjellberg and others, comparing him with Sextus Empiricus on Day 27), Zhuangzi suspends judgement, using paradox to loosen our grip on dogmatic certainty, and finds tranquillity in doing so, rather as the Pyrrhonists found *ataraxia*. This captures the therapeutic tone well.

On a **perspectivist** or 'skill' reading, associated with scholars such as Chris Fraser and Edward Slingerland, the point is practical. Fixed conceptual distinctions make us rigid; the sage is someone who can shift perspectives fluidly and respond to each situation as Cook Ding responds to each joint. What matters is not a theory of truth but a way of moving through the world.

All readings face the **paradox of wu wei**: if effortless action is the goal, how can you *try* to achieve it? Telling someone to be spontaneous is self-defeating. The Daoist answer seems to involve long practice (Ding took years to stop seeing the whole ox) that eventually dissolves itself, like a raft left behind once you reach the shore. The third-century commentator **Guo Xiang** went further, reading Zhuangzi as saying that everything is already 'self-so' and that the sage simply lets each thing fulfil its nature, even within political office, an interpretation that softened Daoism's critique of society.

keyQuote.text: The way that can be spoken of is not the constant way; the name that can be named is not the constant name.
keyQuote.source: Dao De Jing, chapter 1 (trans. after D. C. Lau)

modernConnection.title: Flow, Choking and the Science of Not Trying
modernConnection.body:
In 1990 the psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi published *Flow*, describing the state in which people (surgeons, rock climbers, chess players, musicians) become so absorbed in a challenging task that self-consciousness falls away and action seems to happen by itself. Readers immediately noticed the resemblance to Cook Ding. Flow occurs when skill is well matched to challenge; Ding's knife finds the spaces because years of practice have made his perception exact.

Research on **choking under pressure**, notably by the cognitive scientist Sian Beilock, adds the other half of the Daoist insight. Expert golfers and musicians often perform worse when told to attend closely to the mechanics of what they are doing. Explicit, effortful monitoring interferes with skills that have become automatic. Trying harder can literally make you worse, which is just what the *Dao De Jing* warns about rulers who poke the small fish.

The idea has spread into management (the leader who sets conditions rather than micromanaging, echoing chapter 17), into parenting debates about over-scheduled children, and into design, where empty space and restraint are valued. Edward Slingerland's *Trying Not to Try* (2014) explicitly connects the early Chinese debates to this cognitive science.

But the comparison has limits. Flow is a psychological state that a hit man or a fraudster can enjoy; the Daoist ideal was ethical and cosmological, a way of being in accord with how things are. And the modern self-help version often turns wu wei into a productivity technique, a way to win more at the very competitions Laozi and Zhuangzi mocked. Zhuangzi's useless tree, which lives to a great age precisely because no carpenter wants its twisted wood, is a reminder that the Daoists were questioning the goals, not just the methods, of striving.

vocabulary.definition: The 'Way'; in the Dao De Jing, the nameless source and pattern of all things, prior to language and categories.
vocabulary.example: Because any dao that can be spoken is not the constant Dao, the text proceeds by images and paradoxes.

vocabulary.definition: Virtue or potency; the power a thing or person has when in accord with the Dao.
vocabulary.example: The highest de does not display itself, so it is easy to overlook.

vocabulary.definition: Non-action or effortless action; acting without forcing, striving or self-conscious control.
vocabulary.example: Cook Ding's knife slipping through the joints is a picture of wu wei in skilled action.

vocabulary.definition: 'Self-so'; spontaneity, the way things are of themselves when not interfered with.
vocabulary.example: When the best ruler's work is done, the people say it happened ziran, of itself.

vocabulary.definition: The 'uncarved block'; simplicity and naturalness prior to social shaping.
vocabulary.example: Returning to pu means shedding artificial desires and distinctions.

vocabulary.definition: 'This/not this' or 'right/wrong'; the paired judgements of approval and disapproval that Zhuangzi saw as relative to perspective.
vocabulary.example: The Confucians and Mohists traded shi/fei judgements, each calling right what the other called wrong.

vocabulary.definition: Zhuangzi's term for the ceaseless change of one thing into another, including life into death.
vocabulary.example: The butterfly dream ends by naming the transformation of things.

vocabulary.definition: The puzzle of how one can deliberately try to become someone who acts without trying.
vocabulary.example: Telling an anxious friend 'just relax' runs straight into the paradox of wu wei.

thinkingExercise.title: Where Are You Hacking at the Ox?
thinkingExercise.prompt: Identify an area of your life where effort seems to make things worse, and examine it through Daoist eyes.
steps: Describe one activity where you perform best when absorbed and worst when self-conscious (a sport, conversation, writing, music, sleep).
Describe one area where you are 'hacking' rather than 'carving': pushing against resistance instead of finding the gaps. What would the gaps be?
Apply the paradox of wu wei: what kind of practice might eventually let you stop trying so hard, the way Ding's three years let him stop seeing the whole ox?
Now criticise Daoism: name a situation where not-forcing would be irresponsible or unjust. Does the Daoist have a good reply?

summary: The Dao De Jing is a compiled text of c. 4th–3rd century BCE; the Laozi biography is legend, and the Guodian slips show gradual growth.
The Dao is the nameless, mother-like source and pattern of things; language's fixed names cannot capture it.
Wu wei is effortless, non-forcing action, pictured by water, emptiness and the uncarved block; opposites depend on and reverse into each other.
The text's politics favours minimal, unobtrusive rule, but can also be read as a manual for keeping people simple.
Zhuangzi's butterfly dream, fish debate and critique of shi/fei invite relativist, skeptical and perspectivist readings.
The paradox of wu wei, how to try not to try, links Daoism to modern research on flow and choking.

quiz.question: What pun underlies the opening of the Dao De Jing?
options: Dao also means 'to speak', so the dao that can be dao'd is not the constant Dao
quiz.explanation: Dao means both 'way' and 'to speak'; any way that can be put into words is not the enduring Way.

quiz.question: In chapter 11, what makes a wheel, a pot and a room useful?
quiz.explanation: The hub's hollow, the pot's interior and the room's openings illustrate the use of non-being.

quiz.question: Wu wei means doing nothing at all and withdrawing from activity.
quiz.explanation: Wu wei is non-forcing action; Cook Ding is extremely active, but without strain or self-conscious control.

quiz.question: According to chapter 17, the best kind of ruler is one whom the people:
quiz.explanation: The best rulers are hardly noticed; when their work is done the people say it happened of itself.

quiz.question: How does the Dao De Jing (chapter 38) treat the Confucian virtues of ren, yi and li?
options: As the highest expressions of the Dao
As symptoms of decline after the Dao is lost
quiz.explanation: The text says that when the Dao is lost people fall back on de, then ren, yi and finally li, which marks the beginning of disorder.

quiz.question: How does Zhuangzi's use of dreaming differ from Descartes's?
options: Zhuangzi proves the external world exists
Zhuangzi seeks a certain foundation, Descartes does not
Zhuangzi rejects all dreams as illusions
Descartes uses it to fuel doubt and seek certainty; Zhuangzi seems at ease with the transformation of things
quiz.explanation: Descartes wants to escape doubt; Zhuangzi's dream ends calmly with the 'transformation of things'.

quiz.question: Most scholars think the first seven 'Inner Chapters' of the Zhuangzi are closest to Zhuangzi's own thought.
quiz.explanation: The Inner Chapters are generally considered the core; the Outer and Miscellaneous chapters include later material.

quiz.question: A golfer's putting gets worse when a coach tells her to focus on every detail of her wrist movement. Which Daoist idea does this best illustrate?
options: Wu wei and the danger of forcing skilled action
The uncarved block as a political ideal
quiz.explanation: Self-conscious control disrupting fluent skill is exactly what wu wei warns against, echoed by research on choking.

quiz.question: Which objection is most damaging to a purely relativist reading of Zhuangzi?
options: He clearly values some ways of life, like Cook Ding's, over others
quiz.explanation: If all perspectives were equally valid, Zhuangzi's evident preference for skilful, free living would be groundless.

quiz.question: The Guodian bamboo slips discovered in 1993 contain the complete 81-chapter Dao De Jing in its modern order.
quiz.explanation: They contain roughly a third of the text in a different order, supporting the view that it grew over time.

goDeeper.body:
A central scholarly question is whether the *Dao De Jing* and the *Zhuangzi* belong to one 'school' at all. The term 'Daoist school' (*daojia*) was coined by Han dynasty historians, notably Sima Tan, to classify earlier texts. The two classics differ sharply: the *Dao De Jing* is largely addressed to rulers and offers strategic advice; the *Zhuangzi* mostly mocks political ambition and celebrates individual freedom. Some scholars, like A. C. Graham, thought the *Zhuangzi*'s Inner Chapters may even be earlier than the finished *Dao De Jing*.

A second debate concerns language. Chad Hansen's *A Daoist Theory of Chinese Thought* (1992) argues that classical Chinese thinkers were concerned less with truth and belief than with guiding discourse: which *dao* (way of speaking and acting) to follow. On this view, Zhuangzi's target is not metaphysical truth but the rigid use of names to guide action. Critics like Bryan Van Norden think Hansen exaggerates the differences between Chinese and Greek concerns.

Finally, Daoism has had a long and complicated reception. It shaped Chan (Zen) Buddhism, which you will see in the next lesson; it influenced Heidegger, who worked for a time in 1946 on translating parts of the *Dao De Jing* with the Chinese scholar Paul Shih-yi Hsiao; and it became, through popular books like *The Tao of Pooh*, a staple of Western counterculture. Each appropriation reveals as much about the borrower as about the source, a useful warning for all comparative philosophy.

readings.author: Laozi, trans. D. C. Lau
readings.note: A careful, plain translation with a helpful introduction on the text's composition.

readings.author: Brook Ziporyn (translator)
readings.note: The Inner Chapters with selected commentaries; read chapters 2 and 3.

readings.author: A. C. Graham
readings.note: A classic scholarly history of early Chinese philosophical argument.

questions: Is the paradox of wu wei a fatal flaw or simply a description of how all skills are learned?
Can Daoist political advice be applied to modern states, or does it only fit small agrarian communities?
When Zhuangzi drums on a pot after his wife's death, is this wisdom or emotional evasion?
